sections.title: Spelling and sounds
sections.summary: Polish spelling is regular once you know the extra letters, the two-letter sounds and a few rules about nasal vowels, stress and final consonants. This chapter gives you everything you need to read any Polish word aloud.

rules.title: The alphabet: Latin letters plus nine with marks
rules.body: Polish uses the Latin alphabet plus nine letters with diacritics: ą, ć, ę, ł, ń, ó, ś, ź, ż. The letters q, v and x appear only in foreign words. Every letter is pronounced; there are no silent letters, and spelling is very regular once you know the handful of rules in this chapter.

examples.target: ą ć ę ł ń ó ś ź ż

examples.en: boat (ł like English w, dź like the j in jeans)

rules.title: Digraphs: two letters, one sound
rules.body: Several sounds are written with two letters. sz = English sh (szkoła), cz = ch in church (czas), rz = the sound of ż, like the s in pleasure (rzeka), ch = the same as h (chleb), dz = ds in adds (dzwon), dż = j in jam (dżem), dź = a soft j (dźwięk). Read them as single units; sz is never s followed by z.

rules.title: The nasal vowels ą and ę
rules.body: ą and ę are nasal vowels: ą sounds roughly like the on in French bon, and ę like en. Before b and p they sound like om/em (ząb, zęby); before d, t, c and cz like on/en (kąt, ręka, pięć). At the end of a word ę is pronounced like a plain e in normal speech (proszę sounds like prosze), while final ą keeps its nasal sound (są, mają). Despite its shape, ą is never pronounced like an a.

examples.en: teeth (ę before b sounds like em)

rules.title: ł is w, and w is v
rules.body: The barred ł is pronounced like the English w in water: Łódź, mały, ładny. The plain letter w is always pronounced like English v: woda, Warszawa, wino. Mixing these up is the most common reading mistake for English speakers, so practise them together: ławka (bench) is WAF-ka.

rules.title: Soft consonants and the softening i
rules.body: ś, ź, ć, ń and dź are soft (palatal) consonants, pronounced with the middle of the tongue raised, like sh or ch said with a smile. Before a vowel the same sounds are written with i instead of the accent: ś + a = sia, ć + e = cie, ń + o = nio, ź + e = zie, dź + ę = dzię. So cie in ciebie is simply ć plus e; the i is not a separate vowel. Before a consonant and at the end of a word the accent mark is used (ćma, koń), and before the vowel i nothing extra is needed (ci, si, ni).

examples.en: horse / horses (ń is written ni before e)

rules.title: Same sound, two spellings: ó/u, rz/ż, ch/h
rules.body: Three pairs of spellings are pronounced identically today: ó = u, rz = ż, and ch = h. The spelling reflects history and shows up in related words: ó usually alternates with o in other forms (stół - stoły, Bóg - Boga), and rz usually alternates with r (morze - morski, dworzec - dworca). These pairs are the main source of spelling mistakes even for Poles, so pay attention to them when you learn a new word.

examples.en: God / of God (ó alternates with o)

rules.title: Stress on the second-to-last syllable
rules.body: Polish word stress almost always falls on the penultimate (second-to-last) syllable: dzię-KU-ję, War-SZA-wa, na-u-CZY-ciel, KRA-ków. Exceptions are a few Latin and Greek loanwords stressed on the third-to-last syllable (MU-zy-ka, u-ni-WER-sy-tet, ma-te-MA-ty-ka), and the we/you past-tense forms and conditionals (ro-BI-liś-my, ZRO-bił-bym), where the stress stays where it was before the ending was added.

rules.title: Voiced consonants become voiceless at the end of a word
rules.body: At the end of a word, voiced consonants are pronounced as their voiceless partners: b as p, d as t, g as k, w as f, z as s, ż and rz as sz, dz as c. So chleb sounds like chlep, też like tesz, and Kraków like Krakuf. The spelling keeps the voiced letter, which comes back when an ending follows (chleb - chleba). The same assimilation happens inside clusters: wtorek sounds like ftorek, because t is voiceless.

rules.title: Vowels are short and clear
rules.body: Polish has eight vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u/ó, y, ą, ę) and no long/short distinction. Every vowel is pronounced fully, even in unstressed syllables; there is no uh-reduction as in English. The letter y is a vowel, between the i of bit and the u of but, and it never softens the consonant before it (by, my, ty). The letter i is like ee and always softens the consonant before it (ni, si, ci).

exercises.q: Which English sound does the Polish letter ł represent?
exercises.explain: The barred ł sounds like English w; it is the plain l that sounds like English l.

exercises.q: How is sz pronounced in szkoła?
options: as two sounds, s then z
exercises.explain: sz is a digraph: two letters, one sound, the sh of shoe.

exercises.q: The letter w in Polish is pronounced like English v.
exercises.explain: w is always v (woda = VOH-da); the w sound of English is written ł.

exercises.q: Complete the word for thank you: dzięk___ (three letters)
exercises.explain: dziękuję ends in -uję; the final ę is pronounced like a plain e.

exercises.q: Where does the stress fall in Warszawa?
exercises.explain: Polish stress is on the second-to-last syllable.

exercises.q: The letters ó and u are pronounced the same.
exercises.explain: ó and u are identical in sound; the spelling ó shows that the word has o in related forms (stół - stoły).

exercises.q: Which word contains a nasal vowel?
exercises.explain: ę in ręka is nasal, pronounced roughly like en.

exercises.q: The word for small is pronounced MAH-wy. Spell its last two letters: ma___
exercises.explain: The w sound is written with the barred ł, and the final vowel is y.

exercises.q: How is the final ę of proszę pronounced in normal speech?
exercises.explain: Word-final ę loses its nasality: proszę sounds like prosze.

exercises.q: In chleb (bread) the final b sounds like p.
exercises.explain: Voiced consonants are devoiced at the end of a word, so chleb sounds like chlep.

pairs: soft sh (written si before a vowel)
soft n (written ni before a vowel)
soft ch (written ci before a vowel)
soft zh (written zi before a vowel)

exercises.q: koń means horse. The plural adds -e and the soft ń is spelled with i before a vowel: kon___
exercises.explain: Before a vowel the soft consonant is written with i: ń + e = nie, so konie.

exercises.q: Which vowel letter softens the consonant before it?
exercises.explain: i always softens the preceding consonant (ni, si, ci); y never does.

exercises.q: Polish has silent letters, like the k in the English word knife.
exercises.explain: Every letter in a Polish word is pronounced; there are no silent letters.

exercises.q: The word morze (sea) is pronounced exactly like:
exercises.explain: rz and ż are the same sound, so morze and może (maybe) are homophones.

exercises.q: Fill in the digraph for the zh sound that is spelled with r: ___eka (river)
exercises.explain: rzeka is spelled with rz, which sounds the same as ż.

exercises.q: In zęby (teeth), the ę before b sounds like:
exercises.explain: Before b and p the nasal vowels sound like em/om, so zęby is pronounced zemby.

exercises.q: uniwersytet is stressed on the third-to-last syllable (u-ni-WER-sy-tet), an exception to the usual rule.
exercises.explain: Some Latin and Greek loanwords keep stress on the third-to-last syllable, like uniwersytet and muzyka.

exercises.q: Fill in the digraph for the j of jam: ___em (jam)
exercises.explain: dż is the hard j sound, as in dżem and dżinsy.

exercises.q: Which word begins with an f sound when pronounced?
exercises.explain: Before the voiceless t, the w of wtorek is devoiced to f: ftorek.

exercises.q: Write the first two letters of the word for sister, where the soft ś is spelled with i: ___ostra
exercises.explain: Before a vowel the soft ś is written si: siostra.

exercises.q: y and i stand for the same vowel sound in Polish.
exercises.explain: y is a separate vowel (as in my, ty) and does not soften consonants; i is ee and softens the consonant before it.

exercises.en: Good morning, my name is Anna.

sections.title: Nouns and gender
sections.summary: Every Polish noun has one of three genders, usually visible from its ending, and the gender controls the endings of everything that agrees with it. This chapter shows you how to spot the gender and how to form basic plurals.

rules.title: Three genders, no articles
rules.body: Every Polish noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and there are no words for a or the: dom means a house or the house depending on context. Gender decides the endings of adjectives, pronouns, past-tense verbs and numbers that go with the noun, so learn it with every word. Luckily the ending of the dictionary form (the nominative singular) tells you the gender most of the time.

rules.title: Masculine: ends in a consonant
rules.body: Nouns ending in a consonant are masculine: stół (table), kot (cat), pies (dog), student, komputer, hotel, dzień (day). A few masculine nouns end in -a because they name men: mężczyzna (man), tata (dad), kolega (male friend), poeta (poet), kierowca (driver). They take feminine-looking endings but masculine agreement: ten mężczyzna, dobry kolega.

rules.title: Feminine: ends in -a, -i or a soft consonant
rules.body: Nouns in -a are feminine: kobieta, książka (book), kawa, szkoła, ulica, Polska. Nouns in -i are feminine too (pani, gospodyni). A sizeable group of feminine nouns ends in a soft or hushing consonant and must be memorised: noc (night), sól (salt), twarz (face), rzecz (thing), wieś (village), and every noun in -ość: miłość (love), radość (joy), wiadomość (a piece of news).

rules.title: Neuter: ends in -o, -e, -ę or -um
rules.body: Nouns ending in -o, -e, -ę and -um are neuter: okno (window), miasto (city), piwo (beer), morze (sea), mieszkanie (flat), imię (first name), zwierzę (animal), muzeum, centrum. Nouns in -um are Latin loans and do not change at all in the singular.

rules.title: Three kinds of masculine
rules.body: Masculine nouns split into three subgroups: masculine personal (men: student, brat, lekarz), masculine animate (animals: kot, pies, koń) and masculine inanimate (things: stół, dom, telefon). The distinction matters later: animate and personal nouns take -a in the accusative (widzę kota, znam studenta) while inanimate ones do not change (widzę stół), and masculine personal nouns have their own plural forms (studenci, bracia) and their own form of they (oni).

rules.title: Plural of feminine nouns
rules.body: Feminine nouns in -a replace it with -y: kobieta - kobiety, szkoła - szkoły, lampa - lampy. After k or g the ending is -i: książka - książki, droga - drogi, Polka - Polki. Nouns whose stem ends in a soft or hushing consonant take -e: ulica - ulice, kuchnia - kuchnie, niedziela - niedziele. Feminine nouns ending in a consonant take -e or -y/-i and are best learnt one by one: noc - noce, rzecz - rzeczy, wiadomość - wiadomości.

rules.title: Plural of neuter nouns
rules.body: Neuter nouns in -o and -e replace the ending with -a: okno - okna, miasto - miasta, piwo - piwa, morze - morza, mieszkanie - mieszkania. Nouns in -um also take -a: muzeum - muzea, centrum - centra. Nouns in -ę add a syllable: imię - imiona, zwierzę - zwierzęta. Dziecko (child) is irregular: dzieci.

rules.title: Plural of masculine things and animals
rules.body: Masculine inanimate and animal nouns take -y: stół - stoły, kot - koty, telefon - telefony, sklep - sklepy. After k and g the ending is -i: ptak - ptaki, bank - banki, pociąg - pociągi. Nouns ending in a soft consonant or in c, cz, sz, rz, ż, j, l take -e: koń - konie, hotel - hotele, klucz - klucze, kosz - kosze. Dzień (day) is irregular: dni.

rules.title: Plural of masculine persons
rules.body: Nouns for male persons take -i or -y, often with a change of the final consonant: student - studenci (t becomes ci), Polak - Polacy (k becomes cy), kolega - koledzy (g becomes dzy), mężczyzna - mężczyźni, lekarz - lekarze, nauczyciel - nauczyciele. Some are irregular: brat - bracia, człowiek - ludzie, przyjaciel - przyjaciele. Titles and some family words take -owie: pan - panowie, profesor - profesorowie, syn - synowie, ojciec - ojcowie.

rules.title: Vowel changes when an ending is added
rules.body: A few predictable changes happen when an ending is added. A fleeting e disappears: pies - psy, sen - sny, dzień - dni, ojciec - ojcowie. ó becomes o: stół - stoły, samochód - samochody, ogród - ogrody. ą becomes ę: ząb - zęby, mąż - mężowie. The same changes show up in all the case endings in later chapters, so get used to them now.

exercises.q: What gender is kobieta (woman)?
exercises.explain: Nouns ending in -a are feminine (apart from a few words for men).

exercises.q: What gender is okno (window)?
exercises.explain: Nouns ending in -o are neuter.

exercises.q: Polish has no articles: there is no word for a or the.
exercises.explain: dom can mean a house or the house; context decides.

exercises.q: Plural of kobieta: ___ (women)
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns in -a take -y in the plural.

exercises.q: Which noun is masculine despite ending in -a?
exercises.explain: mężczyzna (man) names a male person, so it is masculine: ten mężczyzna.

exercises.q: noc (night) is masculine because it ends in a consonant.
exercises.explain: noc is one of the feminine nouns ending in a soft or hushing consonant: ta noc.

exercises.q: Plural of okno: ___ (windows)
exercises.explain: Neuter nouns in -o take -a in the plural.

exercises.q: Plural of książka (book):
exercises.explain: After k the plural ending is -i, never -y.

exercises.q: Plural of kot: ___ (cats)
exercises.explain: Masculine animal and thing nouns take -y.

exercises.q: All nouns ending in -ość, like miłość, are feminine.
exercises.explain: The suffix -ość always makes feminine abstract nouns: ta miłość, ta radość.

exercises.q: Which is a masculine animate noun?
exercises.explain: pies (dog) is an animal; the others are things (masculine inanimate).

exercises.q: Plural of pies (dog): ___ (the fleeting e disappears)
exercises.explain: The e of pies drops out before an ending: psy.

exercises.q: Plural of stół (table):
exercises.explain: ó changes to o when an ending is added, and the ending is -y.

exercises.q: muzeum is neuter and does not change in the singular.
exercises.explain: Latin loans in -um are neuter and indeclinable in the singular; the plural is muzea.

exercises.q: Plural of Polak (a Pole): ___
exercises.explain: Masculine personal nouns in -k change k to c and take -y: Polacy.

exercises.q: Plural of imię (first name):
exercises.explain: Nouns in -ę add a syllable in the plural: imię - imiona.

exercises.en: I have two cats and a dog.

exercises.q: The plural of bank is banky.
exercises.explain: After k the ending is -i: banki.

exercises.q: Plural of ząb (tooth): ___
exercises.explain: ą changes to ę when the ending is added: zęby.

exercises.q: Which noun is neuter?
exercises.explain: zwierzę ends in -ę, a neuter ending; kolega is masculine, twarz feminine, hotel masculine.

exercises.q: Plural of nauczyciel (teacher): ___
exercises.explain: Masculine personal nouns in -l take -e: nauczyciele.

exercises.q: Which is the correct nominative plural of lekarz (doctor)?
exercises.explain: Nouns in -rz take -e in the nominative plural; lekarzy is the genitive plural.

exercises.q: pani (Mrs, lady) is a feminine noun.
exercises.explain: Nouns in -i such as pani and gospodyni are feminine.

sections.title: Pronouns and 'to be'
sections.summary: The verb być (to be) is irregular and is the backbone of your first sentences. This chapter covers its forms, the personal and possessive pronouns, why Poles drop subject pronouns, and the polite pan/pani forms.

rules.title: Subject pronouns
rules.body: The subject pronouns are ja (I), ty (you, one person), on (he), ona (she), ono (it), my (we), wy (you, several people), oni / one (they). For things, it is on, ona or ono according to the noun's gender: Gdzie jest stół? On jest tu. (Where is the table? It is here.)

examples.target: Gdzie jest książka? Ona jest tam.
examples.en: Where is the book? It is there.

rules.title: być (to be) in the present
rules.body: jestem (I am), jesteś (you are), jest (he, she, it is), jesteśmy (we are), jesteście (you are), są (they are). Być is irregular, so learn the forms by heart. jest is also used for there is and for weather and feelings: Jest zimno (It is cold).

rules.title: Drop the pronoun
rules.body: Because the verb ending already shows who is doing the action, subject pronouns are normally left out: Jestem studentem, not Ja jestem studentem. Keep them for contrast or emphasis (Ja jestem z Polski, a ona z Anglii), and in short answers (Kto? Ja.). The third-person pronouns on, ona, oni are kept more often, because jest or są alone do not say who.

examples.target: Ja mam czas, a ty nie.
examples.en: I have time, but you don't.

rules.title: oni versus one
rules.body: There are two words for they. oni is used for groups that contain at least one man. one is used for groups of women, children, animals and things: Marek i Anna? Oni są tu. but Anna i Ewa? One są tu. The same split (masculine personal versus everything else) returns in the past tense and in plural adjectives.

examples.en: They (men or a mixed group) are students.

examples.target: Gdzie są klucze? One są na stole.
examples.en: Where are the keys? They are on the table.

rules.title: Formal you: pan, pani, państwo
rules.body: Polish does not use ty with strangers, officials or older people. Instead the nouns pan (sir, Mr) and pani (madam, Mrs) are used with the verb in the third person: Czy pan jest z Warszawy? (Are you from Warsaw?, to a man), Pani jest bardzo miła (You are very kind, to a woman). Plural: panowie (gentlemen), panie (ladies), państwo (a mixed group), with the verb in the plural: Czy państwo są gotowi?

examples.en: Are you (ladies and gentlemen) from Poland?

rules.title: Possessive pronouns
rules.body: my = mój (masculine), moja (feminine), moje (neuter and most plurals): mój dom, moja siostra, moje dziecko. your (ty) = twój, twoja, twoje; our = nasz, nasza, nasze; your (wy) = wasz, wasza, wasze. These agree with the thing possessed, like adjectives. his = jego, her = jej, their = ich never change: jego dom, jego siostra, jej brat, ich dzieci. Formal your uses pana (to a man) or pani (to a woman): Czy to pani torba?

examples.target: mój brat, moja siostra, moje mieszkanie
examples.en: my brother, my sister, my flat

rules.title: To jest... and this/that
rules.body: To introduce or identify things, use to + noun, with or without jest: To (jest) mój brat. To są moje dzieci. This to never changes. Demonstratives that go with a noun do agree with it: ten (masculine), ta (feminine), to (neuter), and in the plural ci (masculine personal) or te (everything else): ten stół, ta kobieta, to okno, ci studenci, te książki. That over there is tamten, tamta, tamto.

rules.title: Negating być
rules.body: Put nie directly before the verb: nie jestem, nie jesteś, nie jest, nie są. Nie jestem z Polski. But there is no / is not here uses the special form nie ma followed by the genitive, not nie jest: Marka nie ma w domu (Marek isn't at home), Nie ma czasu (There is no time).

rules.title: Asking who someone is
rules.body: Kto to jest? (Who is this?), Co to jest? (What is this?). Jak masz na imię? (What is your first name?) is answered with Mam na imię Tomek. Jak się nazywasz? (What is your name?) is answered with Nazywam się Anna Nowak. The formal versions use pan or pani with the third person: Jak pan ma na imię? Jak się pani nazywa?

examples.target: Kto to jest? To jest moja mama.
examples.en: Who is this? This is my mum.

examples.target: Jak masz na imię? Mam na imię Tomek.
examples.en: What's your first name? My first name is Tomek.

exercises.q: I am =
exercises.explain: jestem is the ja form of być.

exercises.q: Oni ___ w domu. (are)
exercises.explain: są is the they form of być.

exercises.q: ona means she.
exercises.explain: on = he, ona = she, ono = it.

exercises.q: Which pronoun do you use for they when talking about a group of women?
exercises.explain: one is used for groups without men; oni only when at least one man is included.

exercises.q: Ty ___ studentem? (are)
exercises.explain: jesteś is the ty form of być.

exercises.q: Polish speakers usually drop subject pronouns like ja because the verb ending already shows the person.
exercises.explain: Jestem already means I am, so ja is added only for emphasis or contrast.

exercises.q: How do you politely ask a man whether he is from Warsaw?
exercises.explain: Formal address to a man uses pan with the verb in the third person; pani is for a woman and ty is informal.

exercises.q: To jest ___ siostra. (my)
exercises.explain: siostra is feminine, so my is moja.

exercises.q: his house =
exercises.explain: jego (his) never changes its form; jej means her.

exercises.q: jego (his) changes its ending to agree with the noun, like mój.
exercises.explain: jego, jej and ich are invariable: jego dom, jego siostra, jego dzieci.

exercises.q: My ___ gotowi. (are, we)
exercises.explain: jesteśmy is the we form of być.

exercises.q: Choose the right word: ___ kobieta jest miła.
exercises.explain: kobieta is feminine, so this is ta.

exercises.q: państwo is used to address a mixed group of men and women politely.
exercises.explain: państwo covers ladies and gentlemen together and takes a plural verb: Czy państwo są gotowi?

exercises.q: Nie ___ zmęczony. (I am not)
exercises.explain: nie goes directly before the verb form jestem.

exercises.q: Anna isn't here =
exercises.explain: Absence is expressed with nie ma plus the genitive, not with nie jest.

exercises.q: Marek i Anna są w domu. ___ są zmęczeni.
exercises.explain: The group includes a man (Marek), so they is oni.

exercises.q: Wy ___ z Anglii? (are, plural you)
exercises.explain: jesteście is the wy form of być.

exercises.q: Jak masz na imię? asks for someone's first name.
exercises.explain: imię is the first name; Jak się nazywasz? asks for the full name or surname.

exercises.q: Which is the correct way to say I am a student?
exercises.explain: The verb must be jestem and the noun after być takes the instrumental ending -em.

exercises.answer: Ci panowie nie są z Polski.
exercises.en: These gentlemen are not from Poland.

exercises.q: Gdzie są klucze? ___ są na stole. (they, for things)
exercises.explain: Keys are things, not male persons, so they is one.

exercises.q: In Czy państwo są gotowi? the verb is in the plural.
exercises.explain: państwo refers to several people and takes są, the plural form.

sections.title: The present tense
sections.summary: Polish has one present tense, formed with six personal endings that fall into three main conjugation classes. This chapter teaches the -am/-asz, -ę/-isz and -ę/-esz patterns plus the most useful irregular verbs.

rules.title: One present tense, three classes
rules.body: Polish has a single present tense that covers English I read, I am reading and I have been reading: Czytam książkę fits all three. It is formed from the stem of an imperfective verb (see chapter 8) with six endings for the six persons; subject pronouns are usually dropped. Verbs fall into three main conjugation classes, named after their ja and ty forms: -am/-asz, -ę/-isz and -ę/-esz.

rules.title: Class 1: -am, -asz (czytać, mieszkać, mieć)
rules.body: Most verbs in -ać follow this pattern: czytać - czytam, czytasz, czyta, czytamy, czytacie, czytają. Other members: mieszkać (live), znać (know a person or place), kochać (love), pamiętać (remember), pytać (ask), śpiewać (sing), grać (play), czekać (wait). mieć (have) belongs here: mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają.

examples.en: They have a lot of time.

rules.title: Class 2: -ę, -isz / -ysz (mówić, robić, lubić, uczyć się)
rules.body: Verbs in -ić, -yć and many in -eć: mówić - mówię, mówisz, mówi, mówimy, mówicie, mówią. After cz, sz, ż and rz the i is written y: uczyć się - uczę się, uczysz się, uczy się; leżeć - leżę, leżysz. Members: robić (do), lubić (like), myśleć (think: myślę, myślisz), dzwonić (phone), palić (smoke), tańczyć (dance), słyszeć (hear: słyszę, słyszysz).

rules.title: Stem changes in class 2 (ja and oni forms)
rules.body: In the ja and oni forms of some class-2 verbs the last consonant of the stem hardens: ś becomes sz (prosić - proszę, prosisz, proszą; nosić - noszę), ź becomes ż (wozić - wożę), dź becomes dz (chodzić - chodzę, chodzisz; widzieć - widzę, widzisz), ć becomes c (płacić - płacę, płacisz), ść becomes szcz (czyścić - czyszczę), źdź becomes żdż (jeździć - jeżdżę, jeździsz). The other four forms keep the soft consonant.

examples.en: A coffee, please. (literally: I ask for coffee)

rules.title: Class 3: -ę, -esz (pisać, pracować, iść, móc, chcieć)
rules.body: pisać - piszę, piszesz, pisze, piszemy, piszecie, piszą. Verbs in -ować change -ow- to -uj-: pracować - pracuję, pracujesz, pracuje, pracujemy, pracujecie, pracują; likewise kupować (buy), studiować, dziękować, gotować, podróżować. Important members with stem changes: iść (go on foot) - idę, idziesz, idzie, idziemy, idziecie, idą; jechać (go by vehicle) - jadę, jedziesz, jedzie, jadą; pić (drink) - piję, pijesz; móc (can) - mogę, możesz, może, możemy, możecie, mogą; chcieć (want) - chcę, chcesz, chce, chcemy, chcecie, chcą.

rules.title: The -em, -esz group: wiedzieć, umieć, rozumieć, jeść
rules.body: A small group has -em in the ja form: umieć (know how to) - umiem, umiesz, umie, umiemy, umiecie, umieją; rozumieć (understand) - rozumiem, rozumiesz, rozumie, rozumiemy, rozumiecie, rozumieją; wiedzieć (know a fact) - wiem, wiesz, wie, wiemy, wiecie, wiedzą; jeść (eat) - jem, jesz, je, jemy, jecie, jedzą. Note the different oni forms: umieją and rozumieją, but wiedzą and jedzą.

examples.en: Do you know where the bank is?

rules.title: znać, wiedzieć, umieć, móc
rules.body: English know and can split four ways. znać = know a person, place or thing (Znam Annę, znam Kraków). wiedzieć = know a fact, used before że, gdzie, kiedy, czy (Wiem, że ona jest tu). umieć = know how to, a learned skill (Umiem gotować). móc = can, be able to or be allowed to (Mogę ci pomóc). Saying Wiem Annę is a typical mistake: a person is known with znać.

examples.en: I don't know where he is.

rules.title: Reflexive verbs with się
rules.body: Many verbs carry the particle się, which never changes its form: nazywać się (be called), uczyć się (learn), bać się (be afraid), cieszyć się (be glad), spotykać się (meet), myć się (wash oneself), interesować się (be interested in). się cannot start a sentence; it usually sits right after the first stressed word or next to the verb: Nazywam się Ewa. Jak się nazywasz? Uczę się polskiego.

rules.title: Present for the near future; idę versus chodzę
rules.body: Present forms with a time expression often refer to the near future, as in English I'm flying tomorrow: Jutro jadę do Krakowa. W sobotę pracuję. Verbs of motion come in pairs: iść / jechać describe one trip in progress or planned (Teraz idę do pracy), while chodzić / jeździć describe a habit or repeated trips (Codziennie chodzę do pracy, Często jeżdżę do Warszawy).

examples.en: I go to Warsaw every week.

sections.title: The cases, part 1: nominative, accusative, genitive
sections.summary: Polish nouns change their endings to show their role in the sentence. This chapter introduces the idea of cases and covers the three most frequent ones: the nominative (subject), the accusative (direct object) and the genitive (possession, 'of', after 'nie ma' and after numbers from five).

rules.title: What cases are
rules.body: Polish nouns, adjectives and pronouns change their endings to show their role in the sentence. There are seven cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, instrumental, locative and vocative. English does this only with pronouns (he, him, his); Polish does it with every noun. The nominative is the dictionary form: it marks the subject and the noun after to jest. This chapter covers the two most frequent cases after the nominative: the accusative and the genitive.

rules.title: Accusative singular: the direct object
rules.body: The accusative marks the direct object (whom? what?). Feminine nouns in -a change it to -ę: kawa - kawę, książka - książkę, Anna - Annę; pani becomes panią, and feminine nouns in a consonant (noc) do not change. Masculine inanimate and all neuter nouns are identical to the nominative: widzę stół, mam okno, piję piwo. Masculine animate nouns (men and animals) add -a: widzę kota, znam studenta, mam brata, mam psa (pies).

examples.en: I have a brother and a dog.

rules.title: Accusative after verbs and prepositions
rules.body: Common verbs taking the accusative: mieć, lubić, kochać, znać, widzieć, czytać, pić, jeść, kupować, oglądać (watch). The accusative is also used after some prepositions of motion and time: na (to an event or open place: na pocztę, na koncert), w / we with days (w sobotę), przez (through; for a period: przez tydzień), o with prosić (prosić o pomoc) and na with czekać (czekać na autobus).

examples.en: I'm going to the post office.

rules.title: Genitive singular endings
rules.body: Masculine nouns take -a or -u: -a for all persons and animals (brata, kota, studenta) and for many concrete objects (chleba, komputera, ołówka), -u for most other things, abstract nouns and loanwords (domu, stołu, sklepu, czasu, hotelu); the choice has to be learnt with the word. Feminine nouns take -y (kawy, kobiety, nocy) or -i after k, g and soft consonants (książki, drogi, kuchni, pani). Neuter nouns take -a (okna, piwa, morza, dziecka).

rules.title: What the genitive does
rules.body: The genitive is the busiest case. It shows possession and of (dom brata, kolor kawy, centrum miasta), quantity (dużo czasu, mało pieniędzy, kilo sera, butelka wody, trochę mleka), and follows many prepositions: do (to, into), z / ze (from, out of), od (from a person; since), bez (without), dla (for), u (at someone's place), obok (next to), koło (near), blisko (close to). Some verbs take it too: szukać (look for), potrzebować (need), słuchać (listen to), uczyć się (learn), bać się (be afraid of).

rules.title: nie ma + genitive and the negated object
rules.body: There isn't / there is no is nie ma plus the genitive: Nie ma mleka (There is no milk), Nie ma Marka (Marek isn't here), Nie ma czasu. When a verb that takes the accusative is negated, its object switches to the genitive: Mam samochód becomes Nie mam samochodu; Lubię kawę becomes Nie lubię kawy; Widzę Annę becomes Nie widzę Anny. Objects in other cases keep their case when negated.

rules.title: Genitive plural
rules.body: Masculine nouns take -ów (studentów, kotów, domów, stołów); masculine nouns ending in a soft or hushing consonant take -i / -y (koni, nauczycieli, kluczy, lekarzy). Feminine and neuter nouns drop their ending entirely: kobieta - kobiet, książka - książek (an e is inserted to break up the cluster), okno - okien, piwo - piw, miasto - miast; soft feminine stems take -i / -y: noc - nocy, kuchnia - kuchni. Irregular: dziecko - dzieci, pieniądze - pieniędzy, rok - lat, człowiek - ludzi, tydzień - tygodni, miesiąc - miesięcy.

rules.title: Numbers: 2-4 take the plural, 5 and up take the genitive
rules.body: After jeden the noun is singular (jeden kot, jedna kawa). After dwa, trzy, cztery the noun is in the nominative plural: dwa koty, trzy książki, cztery okna (two is dwie before feminine nouns: dwie kobiety, dwie kawy). From five upwards, and after dużo, ile, kilka, the noun is in the genitive plural and the verb is singular: pięć kotów, sześć książek, dziesięć okien, Jest pięć osób. Compound numbers ending in 2, 3 or 4 behave like 2-4 (dwadzieścia dwa koty); all others, including those ending in 1, behave like 5 (dwadzieścia jeden kotów). Male persons are special: dwóch, trzech, pięciu studentów.

examples.target: Ile masz lat? Mam dwadzieścia trzy lata.
examples.en: How old are you? I'm twenty-three.

rules.title: Pronouns in the accusative and genitive
rules.body: The personal pronouns have object forms: mnie (me), cię / ciebie (you), go / jego (him; it, masculine), ją (her, accusative) and jej (her, genitive), je (it, neuter, accusative), nas (us), was (you, plural), ich (them, masculine personal; also genitive of all) and je (them, other, accusative). The short forms cię, go are used next to the verb; the long forms ciebie, jego after prepositions and for emphasis: Kocham cię, but Czekam na ciebie. After a preposition him, her, them begin with n-: niego, niej, nich (dla niego, bez niej, do nich).

exercises.explain: nie ma plus the genitive expresses absence.

exercises.explain: Neuter nouns drop the ending, and an e is inserted to break up the cluster: okien.

exercises.explain: After a preposition the long form ciebie is used, not cię.

exercises.explain: szukać (look for) takes the genitive: pracy.

exercises.explain: rok has the irregular genitive plural lat, used after five and higher numbers.

exercises.explain: Compound numbers ending in 2, 3 or 4 behave like dwa, trzy, cztery.

exercises.q: Mam trzy ___ (siostra).
exercises.explain: After trzy the noun is in the nominative plural: siostry.

exercises.q: Czekam na ___ (on). I'm waiting for him.
exercises.explain: After a preposition him is niego, with the n- prefix.

sections.title: The cases, part 2: instrumental, locative, dative
sections.summary: Three more cases you meet every day: the instrumental (jestem nauczycielem, z bratem, autobusem), the locative after w, na and o (w domu, na poczcie, o tobie) and the basics of the dative (daję bratu, podoba mi się).

rules.title: Instrumental singular endings
rules.body: Masculine and neuter nouns take -em (studentem, nauczycielem, oknem, piwem), written -iem after k and g (Polakiem, Anglikiem, słownikiem). Feminine nouns and masculine nouns in -a take -ą (kawą, nauczycielką, Polką, kolegą, mężczyzną); feminine nouns in a consonant also take -ą (nocą, miłością). Adjectives take -ym / -im with masculine and neuter nouns (dobrym, polskim) and -ą with feminine nouns (dobrą).

rules.title: What the instrumental does
rules.body: After być it names a profession, nationality or role: Jestem nauczycielem. Ona jest Polką. On jest moim bratem. After z it means with: kawa z mlekiem, idę z bratem. On its own it expresses the means or tool: jadę autobusem (by bus), piszę długopisem (with a pen). It follows interesować się and zajmować się (Interesuję się muzyką) and gives times of day and seasons: wieczorem, nocą, latem, zimą.

examples.en: I'm going to the cinema with my sister.

rules.title: Instrumental plural
rules.body: The plural ending is -ami for all genders: studentami, kobietami, oknami, książkami, przyjaciółkami. A few nouns take -mi: dziećmi (children), ludźmi (people), przyjaciółmi (friends), pieniędzmi (money), braćmi (brothers). Plural adjectives take -ymi / -imi: z dobrymi przyjaciółmi, z polskimi studentami.

examples.en: I'm going for a walk with the children.

rules.title: Locative: the -e ending with softening
rules.body: The locative is used only after prepositions: w / we (in), na (on, at), o (about), przy (by, at), po (after). Hard-stem nouns take -e and the consonant before it softens: masculine and neuter: sklep - w sklepie, Kraków - w Krakowie, stół - na stole, okno - w oknie, miasto - w mieście, teatr - w teatrze, kino - w kinie, biuro - w biurze; feminine in -a: szkoła - w szkole, Warszawa - w Warszawie, Polska - w Polsce, apteka - w aptece, książka - w książce, siostra - o siostrze. Typical changes: t - cie, d - dzie, r - rze, ł - le, k - ce, g - dze, st - ście.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

rules.title: Locative: the -u and -i / -y endings
rules.body: Masculine and neuter nouns whose stem ends in k, g, ch, a soft consonant, or c, cz, sz, ż, rz, j, l take -u: park - w parku, bank - w banku, hotel - w hotelu, pokój - w pokoju, morze - w morzu, mieszkanie - w mieszkaniu. A few common words take -u irregularly: dom - w domu, syn - o synu, pan - o panu. Feminine nouns with a soft stem or in j take -i (kuchnia - w kuchni, ziemia - na ziemi, pani - o pani, Francja - we Francji); those ending in c, cz, sz, ż, rz take -y (ulica - na ulicy, noc - w nocy, Bydgoszcz - w Bydgoszczy).

examples.en: The children are in the park.

rules.title: w or na?
rules.body: w is used for enclosed spaces, countries and cities: w domu, w szkole, w sklepie, w pracy, w Polsce, w Warszawie. na is used for surfaces, open spaces, events and a fixed set of institutions: na stole, na ulicy, na rynku, na dworcu, na poczcie, na uniwersytecie, na lotnisku, na koncercie, na lekcji, na wsi, and traditionally some regions (na Śląsku, na Węgrzech). Rule of thumb: places you go do + genitive are w + locative (do szkoły / w szkole); places you go na + accusative are na + locative (na pocztę / na poczcie).

examples.en: I am at the post office.

examples.target: Idę do szkoły. Jestem w szkole.
examples.en: I'm going to school. I'm at school.

rules.title: Locative plural and o (about)
rules.body: The locative plural ending is -ach for all genders: w sklepach, w domach, na ulicach, w książkach, w górach (in the mountains), o dzieciach. Plural adjectives take -ych / -ich: w polskich miastach. o + locative means about: Myślę o tobie. Rozmawiamy o pracy. To jest film o wojnie. The locative also gives months after w (w styczniu, in January; see chapter 10) and follows przy (przy stole, at the table) and po (po pracy, after work).

examples.en: We are talking about the children.

rules.title: Dative: to whom?
rules.body: The dative marks the indirect object, the person something is given, said or done to: Daję bratu książkę (I give my brother a book). Verbs that take the dative: pomagać (help), dziękować (thank), podobać się (be pleasing to), ufać (trust), mówić / powiedzieć komuś (tell someone), kupować komuś (buy for someone). Endings: masculine -owi (studentowi, Markowi, nauczycielowi), but a group of common nouns takes -u instead: bratu, ojcu, panu, Bogu, chłopcu, kotu, psu. Feminine nouns take -e with the same softening as the locative (siostrze, mamie, Annie, koleżance) or -i / -y after soft and hushing stems (pani, Marii, nocy). Neuter nouns take -u (dziecku, miastu).

examples.en: I'm giving my brother a present.
I'm buying the child an ice cream.

rules.title: Dative pronouns and impersonal expressions
rules.body: The dative pronouns are mi (long form mnie), ci (tobie), mu (jemu), jej, nam, wam, im. Short forms go next to the verb and never start a sentence. Podoba mi się Kraków (I like Krakow, literally Krakow is pleasing to me). Dziękuję ci. Pomagam mu. Formal: Dziękuję panu / pani. The dative also shows who experiences a state: Jest mi zimno (I am cold), Jest nam miło (We are pleased), Trudno mi powiedzieć (It's hard for me to say), Smutno jej (She is sad).

examples.en: Pleased to meet you. (literally: it is pleasant to me)

rules.title: Pronouns in the instrumental and locative
rules.body: Instrumental: mną, tobą, nim, nią, nami, wami, nimi. With z the form ze is used before mną: ze mną (with me), but z tobą, z nim, z nią, z nami, z wami, z nimi. Locative (always after a preposition): o mnie, o tobie, o nim, o niej, o nas, o was, o nich. Possessives follow the adjective endings: z moim bratem, z moją siostrą, o moim bracie, o mojej siostrze, z naszymi dziećmi.

exercises.explain: After być a profession takes the instrumental: masculine -em.

exercises.q: Ona jest ___ (Polka). She is Polish.
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns take -ą in the instrumental.

exercises.q: After być, a noun naming a profession or nationality takes the instrumental case.

exercises.explain: z meaning with takes the instrumental; after k the ending is -iem.

exercises.q: Mieszkam w ___ (Kraków). I live in Krakow.
exercises.explain: Locative -e with softening: w becomes wi, and ó changes to o.

exercises.en: I go to work by bus.

exercises.q: w Warszawie is the locative of Warszawa.
exercises.explain: Feminine -a nouns with a hard stem take -e and soften: w - wi, so Warszawie.

exercises.q: On jest moim ___ (brat).
exercises.explain: After być the noun takes the instrumental: bratem.

exercises.q: Interesuję się ___ (muzyka). I'm interested in music.
exercises.explain: interesować się takes the instrumental: muzyką.

exercises.q: in the park =
exercises.explain: Masculine nouns ending in k take -u in the locative.

exercises.q: Książka jest na ___ (stół). The book is on the table.
exercises.explain: Locative -e with ł softening to l and ó changing to o: na stole.

exercises.en: I think about you every day.

exercises.q: After na meaning at or on (location, not motion) the noun is in the locative case.
exercises.explain: na stole, na poczcie, na uniwersytecie are locatives; na with motion takes the accusative.

exercises.q: Which preposition? Jestem ___ uniwersytecie.
exercises.explain: uniwersytet belongs to the group of institutions that take na.

exercises.q: Daję ___ (brat) prezent. I'm giving my brother a present.
exercises.explain: brat is one of the common nouns with dative -u instead of -owi.

exercises.q: Thank you, said formally to a woman:
exercises.explain: dziękować takes the dative; the dative of pani is pani, and panu is for a man.

exercises.q: pomagać (to help) takes the dative: Pomagam mamie.
exercises.explain: pomagać, dziękować and podobać się all take the dative.

exercises.q: Podoba ___ się Kraków. (I like Krakow: dative of ja)
exercises.explain: podobać się takes the dative of the person who likes: mi.

exercises.q: Rozmawiam ze ___ (studenci).
exercises.explain: z / ze (with) takes the instrumental; the plural ending is -ami.

exercises.q: Mieszkam w ___ (Polska). I live in Poland.
exercises.explain: sk softens to sc before the locative -e: w Polsce.

exercises.q: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explain: The instrumental of ja is mną, and z becomes ze before it.

exercises.q: The locative case is used only after prepositions.
exercises.explain: The locative always follows w, na, o, przy or po; it never stands alone.

exercises.q: Opowiadam o ___ (dzieci). I'm talking about the children.
exercises.explain: The locative plural ending is -ach: dzieciach.

exercises.q: Dative of siostra:
exercises.explain: Feminine dative takes -e with softening: r becomes rz, so siostrze.

exercises.q: Jadę ___ (pociąg). I'm going by train.
exercises.explain: Means of transport take the instrumental; after g the ending is -iem.

exercises.q: In Nie ma go w domu, the phrase w domu is in the genitive.
exercises.explain: w domu is the locative (after w); only go (him) is in the genitive because of nie ma.

sections.title: Adjectives and agreement
sections.summary: Adjectives change their ending to match the gender, number and case of their noun. This chapter gives the basic endings, the comparative and superlative, irregular forms like lepszy and gorszy, and how to turn adjectives into adverbs.

rules.title: Agreement and the dictionary form
rules.body: Adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number and case. The dictionary form is the masculine nominative singular, which ends in -y (dobry, nowy, stary, duży, ciekawy) or in -i after k, g and soft consonants (polski, drogi, wysoki, tani, ostatni).

rules.title: Singular nominative endings
rules.body: Masculine: -y / -i (dobry kot, polski film). Feminine: -a (dobra kawa, polska muzyka, tania książka). Neuter: -e, written -ie after k and g and after soft stems (dobre piwo, polskie miasto, drogie wino, tanie mieszkanie). The same endings are used after być: Film jest dobry. Kawa jest dobra. Piwo jest dobre.

examples.target: dobry kot, dobra kawa, dobre piwo
examples.en: a good cat, good coffee, good beer

examples.target: polski film, polska muzyka, polskie miasto
examples.en: a Polish film, Polish music, a Polish city

rules.title: Plural nominative endings
rules.body: With masculine personal nouns (men, mixed groups) the ending is -i / -y and the final consonant often changes: dobrzy studenci, polscy lekarze, mili panowie, starzy ludzie, młodzi, wysocy, drodzy przyjaciele. With all other nouns (women, animals, things) the ending is -e / -ie: dobre koty, nowe książki, polskie miasta, małe dzieci, miłe kobiety. The split is the same as oni / one.

examples.target: Oni są mili. One są miłe.
examples.en: They (men) are nice. They (women) are nice.

rules.title: Position of the adjective
rules.body: A descriptive adjective normally comes before the noun: duży dom, ciekawa książka, stare miasto. It follows the noun in fixed terms that classify the thing rather than describe it: język polski (the Polish language), dworzec kolejowy (railway station), sok pomarańczowy (orange juice), Unia Europejska, Morze Bałtyckie. Dictionaries and signs often show this noun-first order.

rules.title: Adjective endings in the other cases
rules.body: Masculine and neuter singular: genitive -ego (dobrego, polskiego), dative -emu, instrumental and locative -ym / -im (dobrym, polskim). Feminine singular: accusative -ą (dobrą kawę), instrumental -ą (z dobrą koleżanką), genitive, dative and locative -ej (dobrej kawy, o dobrej kawie). Masculine animate accusative equals the genitive: widzę dobrego kota. Plural: genitive and locative -ych / -ich (dobrych, polskich), instrumental -ymi / -imi, and the masculine personal accusative equals the genitive (znam dobrych studentów).

examples.en: I live in a small flat.
I'm talking to a new (female) friend.

rules.title: The comparative
rules.body: Add -szy to the stem: nowy - nowszy, stary - starszy, młody - młodszy, tani - tańszy, ciekawy - ciekawszy, or -ejszy after a group of consonants: ładny - ładniejszy, ciepły - cieplejszy, trudny - trudniejszy, łatwy - łatwiejszy. Longer adjectives and participles use bardziej (more) and mniej (less): bardziej interesujący, mniej zmęczony. Than is niż + nominative or od + genitive: Marek jest wyższy niż Tomek = Marek jest wyższy od Tomka.

examples.en: Today it is warmer than yesterday.

rules.title: The superlative
rules.body: Put naj- in front of the comparative: najnowszy, najstarszy, najładniejszy, najtańszy, najbardziej interesujący. The most ... in / of is w + locative or z + genitive: najlepsza restauracja w mieście, najmłodszy z braci. The superlative declines like any adjective: w najstarszym mieście, najlepszą kawę.

examples.target: To jest najstarszy kościół w Polsce.
examples.en: This is the oldest church in Poland.
She is the youngest of the sisters.
This is the most interesting book.

rules.title: Irregular comparison
rules.body: A few very common adjectives change their stem: dobry - lepszy - najlepszy (good, better, best), zły - gorszy - najgorszy (bad, worse, worst), duży / wielki - większy - największy (big), mały - mniejszy - najmniejszy (small), wysoki - wyższy (tall), niski - niższy (short, low), drogi - droższy (expensive), lekki - lżejszy (light), długi - dłuższy (long), ciężki - cięższy (heavy), krótki - krótszy (short), szeroki - szerszy (wide).

rules.title: Adverbs: -o and -e
rules.body: Adverbs are made from adjectives with -o (szybki - szybko, tani - tanio, drogi - drogo, ciepły - ciepło, zimny - zimno, miły - miło) or with -e plus softening, especially for adjectives in -ny and for dobry and zły (dobry - dobrze, zły - źle, ładny - ładnie, świetny - świetnie, wolny - wolno). Comparative adverbs end in -ej (szybciej, taniej, drożej, ładniej, cieplej) with irregular lepiej (better), gorzej (worse), więcej (more), mniej (less); the superlative adds naj- (najszybciej, najlepiej). Adverbs also describe states: Jest zimno. Jest mi dobrze.

rules.title: Asking about qualities: jaki, który, jak
rules.body: jaki / jaka / jakie asks what kind of or what is something like, and agrees with the noun: Jaki jest ten film? Jaka jest pogoda? Jakie jest piwo? The answer is an adjective: Ciekawy. Ładna. Dobre. który / która / które asks which one: Która książka? W którym roku? jak asks how and is answered with an adverb: Jak mówisz po polsku? Dobrze.

examples.en: What is this hotel like? Expensive.

exercises.q: ___ kawa (dobry)
exercises.explain: kawa is feminine, so the adjective takes -a.

exercises.q: To jest ___ film. (polski)
exercises.explain: film is masculine, so the dictionary form polski is used.

exercises.q: Adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number and case.
exercises.explain: dobry kot, dobra kawa, dobre piwo, dobrej kawy: the ending changes with the noun.

exercises.q: polski + miasto (city) =
exercises.explain: miasto is neuter; after k the neuter ending is -ie.

exercises.q: Te książki są ___. (nowy)
exercises.explain: Books are not male persons, so the plural ending is -e.

exercises.q: Comparative of stary (old):
exercises.explain: Short adjectives add -szy: starszy.

exercises.q: Piję ___ kawę. (dobry, accusative feminine)
exercises.explain: The feminine accusative of an adjective ends in -ą.

exercises.q: The comparative of dobry is dobrzejszy.
exercises.explain: dobry is irregular: lepszy, najlepszy.

exercises.q: These students (men) are nice =
exercises.explain: Masculine personal plural: ci and mili (ł softens to l before -i).

exercises.q: Marek jest ___ niż Tomek. (wysoki, comparative)
exercises.explain: wysoki has the irregular comparative wyższy.

exercises.answer: To jest najlepsza restauracja w mieście.
exercises.en: This is the best restaurant in town.

exercises.q: Adverb from szybki (fast):
exercises.explain: Most adverbs are formed with -o: szybko.

exercises.q: dobrze is the adverb of dobry.
exercises.explain: dobry - dobrze and zły - źle use the -e ending with softening.

exercises.q: Ona mówi ___ po polsku. (dobry, as an adverb)
exercises.explain: How she speaks calls for the adverb dobrze, not the adjective dobra.

exercises.q: In which phrase is the adjective normally placed after the noun?
exercises.explain: Classifying terms like język polski and sok pomarańczowy put the adjective after the noun; descriptive adjectives go before.

exercises.q: Nie znam tego ___ pana. (stary, genitive masculine)
exercises.explain: Masculine genitive singular of an adjective ends in -ego.

exercises.q: Long adjectives like interesujący usually form the comparative with bardziej.
exercises.explain: bardziej interesujący, bardziej zmęczony; the suffix -szy is for short adjectives.

exercises.q: Superlative of ładny (pretty):
exercises.explain: naj- goes in front of the comparative ładniejszy.

exercises.en: Today it is warmer than yesterday.

exercises.q: Mieszkam w ___ mieszkaniu. (mały, locative neuter)
exercises.explain: Masculine and neuter locative of adjectives is -ym / -im.

exercises.q: What is the weather like? =
exercises.explain: pogoda is feminine, so what kind is jaka.

exercises.q: After od in a comparison (wyższy od Tomka) the noun is in the genitive.
exercises.explain: od always takes the genitive; niż takes the nominative instead.

exercises.q: To jest ___ samochód niż tamten. (drogi, comparative)
exercises.explain: drogi has the irregular comparative droższy.

exercises.q: Rozmawiam z ___ koleżanką. (nowy, instrumental feminine)
exercises.explain: Feminine instrumental of an adjective ends in -ą, matching koleżanką.

exercises.q: Ci ___ panowie są z Krakowa. (stary, masculine personal plural)
exercises.explain: Before the masculine personal -y, r changes to rz: starzy.

exercises.q: polskie is used with neuter singular nouns and with all plurals except masculine personal ones.
exercises.explain: polskie miasto, polskie miasta, polskie kobiety, but polscy studenci.

sections.title: Past tense and aspect
sections.summary: The Polish past tense is regular but marks gender as well as person, and almost every verb comes in an imperfective/perfective pair. This chapter builds the past tense from the ł-forms and explains how to choose the aspect.

rules.title: Building the past tense
rules.body: Take the infinitive, drop -ć, add ł and then the person-and-gender endings. Singular: masculine -łem, -łeś, -ł; feminine -łam, -łaś, -ła; neuter -ło (third person only). Plural: masculine personal (groups with men) -liśmy, -liście, -li; all other groups -łyśmy, -łyście, -ły. robić: robiłem / robiłam, robiłeś / robiłaś, robił / robiła / robiło, robiliśmy / robiłyśmy, robiliście / robiłyście, robili / robiły.

examples.en: they (with men) did, they (women / things) did

rules.title: być in the past
rules.body: byłem / byłam, byłeś / byłaś, był / była / było, byliśmy / byłyśmy, byliście / byłyście, byli / były. Byłem wczoraj w kinie. Gdzie byłaś? Było zimno. The past of nie ma (there is no) is nie było plus the genitive: Nie było czasu. Nie było Marka.

examples.en: Yesterday I (a man) was at work.

rules.title: Vowel changes: -eć and -ąć verbs
rules.body: Verbs in -eć have a before ł in most forms but keep e in the masculine personal plural: mieć - miałem, miałaś, miał, miała, miało, miały, but mieli; chcieć - chciałem, chciała, chcieli; widzieć - widziałem, widzieli; rozumieć - rozumiałem, rozumieli; musieć - musiałem, musieli. Verbs in -ąć have ą only in the masculine singular and ę everywhere else: wziąć - wziąłem, wziął, but wzięłam, wzięła, wzięli, wzięły; zacząć - zacząłem, zaczął, zaczęła, zaczęli.

examples.en: I had time. We had time.

examples.target: Ona chciała kawę. Oni chcieli kawę.
examples.en: She wanted coffee. They wanted coffee.
I (m) took the keys. She took the keys.

rules.title: Irregular past forms
rules.body: iść (go): szedłem, szedłeś, szedł; szłam, szłaś, szła; szliśmy, szliście, szli; szłyśmy, szłyście, szły; the same in compounds: przyszedł, przyszła, poszli. móc (can): mogłem, mógł, mogła, mogli, mogły. jeść (eat): jadłem, jadł, jadła, jedli, jadły. nieść (carry): niósł, niosła, nieśli. znaleźć (find): znalazłem, znalazł, znalazła, znaleźli. usiąść (sit down): usiadł, usiadła, usiedli.

rules.title: Movable endings
rules.body: The person endings -em, -eś, -śmy, -ście can detach from the verb and attach to an earlier word, usually a question word or conjunction: Gdzie byłeś? = Gdzieś był? Co robiliście? = Coście robili? Dlaczego nie przyszłaś? = Dlaczegoś nie przyszła? This is colloquial and regional; you need to recognise it, but the forms with the ending on the verb are always correct and are the ones to use.

rules.title: Aspect: imperfective and perfective
rules.body: Almost every Polish verb comes in a pair. The imperfective verb presents an action as a process, a habit, a duration or something ongoing, with no focus on completion. The perfective verb presents one action as completed, with a result. Both have a past tense: Czytałem tę książkę (I was reading / used to read this book) against Przeczytałem tę książkę (I read it through, I finished it). Only imperfective verbs have a present tense; the present-looking forms of a perfective verb refer to the future: Przeczytam = I will read it (to the end).

examples.en: I read this book (and finished it). (perfective)
I am writing a letter. I will write a letter.

rules.title: How aspect pairs are formed
rules.body: Three patterns. (1) A prefix makes the perfective: pisać - napisać, czytać - przeczytać, robić - zrobić, jeść - zjeść, pić - wypić, dzwonić - zadzwonić, gotować - ugotować, płacić - zapłacić. (2) A different suffix: kupować - kupić, dawać - dać, otwierać - otworzyć, zamykać - zamknąć, zaczynać - zacząć, kończyć - skończyć, spotykać - spotkać, wracać - wrócić, pomagać - pomóc. (3) Different roots: brać - wziąć (take), mówić - powiedzieć (say), widzieć - zobaczyć (see), kłaść - położyć (put), iść - pójść (go). Learn each verb together with its partner.

examples.en: to speak, say - to say (once, completed)

rules.title: Choosing the aspect in the past
rules.body: Use the imperfective for background, duration, habits and what was going on: Wczoraj cały dzień czytałem (I spent all day reading). Signal words: zawsze, często, codziennie, zwykle, długo, cały dzień, kiedyś. Use the perfective for a single completed event, a result, or a sequence of actions one after another: Wczoraj napisałem list i wysłałem go (I wrote a letter and sent it). Signal words: już, w końcu, nagle, raz, wreszcie, a question like Czy zrobiłeś? (Did you get it done?).

examples.target: Zwykle wstawałem o siódmej, ale dzisiaj wstałem o ósmej.
examples.en: I usually got up at seven, but today I got up at eight.
While I was reading, the phone rang.

examples.target: Czy zrobiłaś zadanie? Tak, już zrobiłam.
examples.en: Did you do the homework? Yes, I've already done it.

rules.title: Aspect and the future
rules.body: The perfective future looks like a present tense: napiszę, zrobię, kupię, pójdę, zadzwonię, przeczytam. The imperfective future is compound: będę + infinitive, or będę + the ł-form agreeing in gender: będę pisać or będę pisał / pisała; będziesz, będzie, będziemy, będziecie, będą. Będę czytać cały wieczór (process) versus Przeczytam to jutro (completion).

examples.en: I will be working all day.

rules.title: Time expressions with the past
rules.body: wczoraj (yesterday), przedwczoraj (the day before yesterday), w zeszłym tygodniu (last week), w zeszłym roku (last year), w zeszłą sobotę (last Saturday), dwa dni temu (two days ago), rok temu (a year ago), dawno temu (long ago), kiedyś (once, some time ago), nigdy (never, with nie). temu follows the length of time, as English ago does.

examples.en: I (f) was in Poland a year ago.
I (m) have never been to Krakow.

exercises.q: I (a man) was =
exercises.explain: The masculine first-person singular ending is -łem.

exercises.q: Wczoraj ___ w kinie. (być, I, a woman)
exercises.explain: The feminine first-person singular ending is -łam.

exercises.q: The past tense endings show the gender of the subject.
exercises.explain: robił (he), robiła (she), robiło (it): the ł-form agrees in gender.

exercises.q: Oni ___ w Krakowie. (mieszkać)
exercises.explain: oni (masculine personal) takes -li; one would take -ły.

exercises.q: Ona ___ list. (pisać)
exercises.explain: Third person feminine ends in -ła: pisała.

exercises.q: Past of mieć for they (men):
exercises.explain: -eć verbs keep e in the masculine personal plural: mieli, but miały for other groups.

exercises.q: Ona ___ kawę. (chcieć)
exercises.explain: chcieć: the e becomes a before ł in the singular: chciała.

exercises.q: Oni chcieli is correct and oni chciali is wrong.
exercises.explain: The masculine personal plural of -eć verbs keeps e: chcieli, mieli, widzieli.

exercises.q: Which verb is perfective?
exercises.explain: The prefix na- makes napisać the perfective partner of pisać.

exercises.q: Marek ___ do domu. (iść, past, he)
exercises.explain: iść is irregular in the past: szedł (he), szła (she), szli (they).

exercises.en: I (a woman) have never been to Poland.

exercises.q: Perfective verbs have a present-tense meaning.
exercises.explain: The present-looking forms of a perfective verb (napiszę, zrobię) refer to the future.

exercises.q: I read the whole book (and finished it) =
exercises.explain: A completed action in the past takes the perfective past: przeczytałem.

exercises.q: My (women) ___ w domu. (być)
exercises.explain: A group without men takes -łyśmy.

exercises.q: Przeczytam means:
exercises.explain: przeczytać is perfective, so its present-looking form is a future.

exercises.q: codziennie (every day) usually goes with an imperfective verb.
exercises.explain: Habits and repeated actions are expressed with the imperfective: Codziennie czytałem gazetę.

exercises.q: Wczoraj ___ nowy telefon. (kupić, I, a man)
exercises.explain: One completed purchase: perfective kupić, masculine -łem.

exercises.en: What were you (to a woman) doing yesterday evening?

exercises.q: Past of móc, he could:
exercises.explain: móc: mógł (he), mogła (she), mogli (they); mógłem is I could.

exercises.q: Ona ___ obiad. (zjeść)
exercises.explain: jeść has the irregular past jadł / jadła; zjeść adds the prefix: zjadła.

exercises.q: Będę czytać is the future of the imperfective verb czytać.
exercises.explain: Imperfective verbs form the future with będę plus the infinitive or ł-form.

exercises.q: Zwykle ___ o siódmej, ale dzisiaj ___ o ósmej. (wstawać / wstać, I, a man)
exercises.explain: zwykle (usually) calls for the imperfective wstawałem; the single event today takes the perfective wstałem.

exercises.q: Oni ___ pracę o ósmej. (zacząć)
exercises.explain: -ąć verbs have ę outside the masculine singular: zaczęli.

exercises.q: Gdzieś był? is a colloquial version of:
exercises.explain: The ending -eś has moved from byłeś onto gdzie.

exercises.q: Dwa lata ___ mieszkałem w Londynie. (ago)
exercises.explain: temu follows the length of time, like English ago.

exercises.q: In Nie było czasu, the noun is in the genitive.
exercises.explain: nie było is the past of nie ma and takes the genitive like it.

sections.title: Questions, negation and word order
sections.summary: Polish asks yes/no questions with czy, declines its question words, piles up negatives (nikt nic nie wie) and moves words around to show what is new information. This chapter covers all of that plus the placement of little words like się and go.

rules.title: Yes/no questions with czy
rules.body: Put czy at the start of a statement; the word order does not change: Czy mówisz po polsku? Czy to jest twój brat? In speech czy is often dropped and rising intonation alone marks the question: Mówisz po polsku? Answer with tak or nie, usually repeating the verb: Tak, mówię. Nie, nie mówię.

examples.en: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: kto (who), co (what), gdzie (where), dokąd (where to), skąd (where from), kiedy (when), dlaczego (why), jak (how), ile (how much, how many), jaki / jaka / jakie (what kind of), który (which), czyj / czyja / czyje (whose). kto takes a masculine singular verb even when the answer is a woman: Kto to był? Kto przyszedł? co takes the neuter: Co się stało? ile is followed by the genitive plural: Ile masz lat? Ile to kosztuje?

rules.title: Question words decline
rules.body: kto and co change with the case: kto - kogo (accusative and genitive), komu (dative), kim (instrumental and locative); co - czego (genitive), czemu (dative), czym (instrumental and locative). Kogo widzisz? Kogo nie ma? Komu pomagasz? Z kim idziesz? O czym myślisz? Czego szukasz? jaki and który decline like adjectives: Jaką kawę lubisz? W którym roku? A preposition stays in front of the question word: Z kim? O czym? Do kogo?

examples.en: Who are you going to the cinema with?

rules.title: Negation with nie
rules.body: nie comes directly before the verb and is written separately from it: Nie wiem. Nie lubię kawy. Nie ma go. With a negated verb the direct object goes into the genitive (chapter 5). nie with adjectives, adverbs and nouns is written together with them: niedobry (not good), nieładnie, nieprawda, except when there is a contrast: nie duży, ale mały.

rules.title: Multiple negation is required
rules.body: When a sentence contains nikt (nobody), nic (nothing), nigdy (never), nigdzie (nowhere), żaden (no, none) or ani... ani (neither... nor), the verb must still take nie: Nikt nie wie. Nic nie rozumiem. Nigdy tam nie byłem. Nie mam żadnych pieniędzy. Nie lubię ani kawy, ani herbaty. The negatives decline: nikt - nikogo, nikomu, nikim; nic - niczego / nic, niczemu, niczym. Nikogo nie ma (There is nobody here). Nikt nic nie wie (Nobody knows anything).

examples.en: I have never been to Paris.

rules.title: Short answers, softeners and tags
rules.body: Tak. / Nie. A verb is often repeated: Masz czas? Mam. / Nie mam. Softer answers: Nie, dziękuję. Niestety nie (Unfortunately not). Chyba tak (I think so). Oczywiście (Of course). Tag questions add prawda?, nie? or tak? at the end: Jesteś z Polski, prawda? czy also means whether in indirect questions: Nie wiem, czy on przyjdzie.

examples.en: Do you like coffee? I do.
I don't know whether she will come.

rules.title: Flexible word order and new information
rules.body: Because cases show who does what to whom, the order of words can change without changing the basic meaning. The neutral order is subject - verb - object: Marek pije kawę. Known information (the topic) comes first, and the new or most important information (the focus) goes at the end: Kawę pije Marek answers Kto pije kawę? (It is Marek who drinks the coffee), while Marek pije kawę answers Co robi Marek? Time and place adverbs usually go first or before the verb: Wczoraj Marek pił kawę w domu.

examples.en: It's Marek who is drinking the coffee.

examples.target: Kto to zrobił? Zrobiła to Anna.

rules.title: Where the little words go
rules.body: Short pronouns (mi, ci, go, mu, cię, ją) and się are unstressed clitics: they cannot begin a sentence and are avoided at the very end of longer sentences. They sit after the first stressed word or next to the verb: Jak się masz? (not Jak masz się?). Bardzo cię lubię (better than Lubię cię bardzo). Nie znam go. Podoba mi się. For emphasis use the long forms at the front: Jego nie znam. Ciebie lubię. nie stays directly before the verb, and a preposition never separates from its noun.

examples.target: Jego nie znam, ale ją znam.
examples.en: Him I don't know, but her I do.

rules.title: Two objects and the position of adjectives
rules.body: Adjectives go before their noun unless they classify it (język polski). When a verb has two objects, the indirect object (dative) usually precedes the direct object: Daję bratu książkę. With pronouns the known thing comes first and the new one last: Daję mu ją. Daję ją bratu (I give it to my brother). Question words come first, and czy only ever stands at the start of a question or an indirect question.

examples.en: I'm giving my brother a book.

rules.title: Linking words and commas
rules.body: i (and), a (and / whereas, for contrast), ale (but), bo (because), więc (so), że (that), czy (whether), który (which, who), jeśli (if), kiedy (when), żeby (in order to, so that), dlatego (that's why). Polish puts a comma before że, bo, który, czy, jeśli, kiedy, żeby, ale and a: Wiem, że jesteś zmęczony. Nie idę, bo pada. To jest pan, który tu mieszka. Ja jestem z Polski, a ona z Anglii.

examples.en: I know that you are tired.
I'm not going, because it's raining.

examples.target: To jest kobieta, która tu pracuje.
examples.en: This is the woman who works here.

examples.target: Lubię kawę, a on lubi herbatę.
examples.en: I like coffee, whereas he likes tea.

exercises.q: Which word turns a statement into a yes/no question?
exercises.explain: czy at the start of a statement makes it a yes/no question.

exercises.q: ___ mówisz po angielsku? (Do you speak English?)
exercises.explain: czy opens the question; the rest of the sentence keeps its order.

exercises.q: nie goes directly before the verb: Nie wiem.
exercises.explain: nie is placed immediately before the verb and written as a separate word.

exercises.q: Nobody knows =
exercises.explain: nikt requires nie before the verb: double negation is compulsory.

exercises.q: Nigdy ___ byłem w Paryżu. (I have never been to Paris)
exercises.explain: nigdy must be accompanied by nie before the verb.

exercises.q: Polish requires double negation: Nic nie rozumiem.
exercises.explain: nic (nothing) and nie together are the only correct way to say I don't understand anything.

exercises.q: Where from? =
exercises.explain: skąd = where from, dokąd = where to, gdzie = where.

exercises.q: ___ to kosztuje? (How much does it cost?)
exercises.explain: ile asks how much or how many.

exercises.q: Z ___ idziesz do kina? (With whom)
exercises.explain: z (with) takes the instrumental, and the instrumental of kto is kim.

exercises.q: Jak masz się? is the normal word order for How are you?
exercises.explain: się goes after the first stressed word: Jak się masz?

exercises.q: O ___ myślisz? (What are you thinking about?)
exercises.explain: o (about) takes the locative; the locative of co is czym.

exercises.q: Answering Kto pije kawę?, which order puts the new information (Marek) in its usual end position?
exercises.explain: The new or most important information goes to the end: Kawę pije Marek.

exercises.q: Nie mam ___ pieniędzy. (żaden, genitive plural)
exercises.explain: żaden agrees with the genitive plural noun: żadnych pieniędzy.

exercises.q: kto takes a feminine verb when it refers to a woman: Kto przyszła?
exercises.explain: kto always takes the masculine singular: Kto przyszedł?, even if a woman came.

exercises.q: I don't know whether he will come =
exercises.explain: In an indirect question whether is czy, not że or jeśli.

exercises.en: I don't know whether she will come.

exercises.q: Jesteś z Polski, ___? (tag question: right?)
exercises.explain: prawda?, nie? or tak? at the end turns a statement into a tag question.

exercises.q: Which sentence has the correct position of cię?
exercises.explain: cię is a clitic: it cannot start a sentence and sits after the first stressed word.

exercises.q: A comma is placed before że in Wiem, że jesteś zmęczony.
exercises.explain: Polish always puts a comma before że, bo, który, czy and jeśli.

exercises.q: ___ nie ma w domu. (Nobody is at home: nikt, genitive)
exercises.explain: nie ma takes the genitive, and the genitive of nikt is nikogo.

exercises.q: Nie lubię ani kawy, ani herbaty means:
options: I like neither coffee nor tea.
I like either coffee or tea.
I don't like coffee but I like tea.
I like both coffee and tea.
exercises.explain: ani... ani with nie means neither... nor.

exercises.q: ___ jest twoja siostra? (Where)
exercises.explain: gdzie asks where (location).

exercises.q: nie is written together with verbs: niewiem.
exercises.explain: nie is always a separate word before a verb: nie wiem; it is joined only to adjectives, adverbs and nouns.

exercises.q: ___ pomagasz? (Whom are you helping?)
exercises.explain: pomagać takes the dative, and the dative of kto is komu.

exercises.q: ___ jest ta książka? (Whose)
exercises.explain: czyj agrees with the noun: książka is feminine, so czyja.

sections.title: Numbers, time and dates
sections.summary: Numbers in Polish interact with case and gender, and time, days and dates each use their own fixed patterns of ordinals and cases. This chapter covers counting, telling the time, the days and months, and saying dates and years.

rules.title: Cardinal numbers 0-19
rules.body: zero, jeden, dwa, trzy, cztery, pięć, sześć, siedem, osiem, dziewięć, dziesięć; then 11-19 add -naście: jedenaście, dwanaście, trzynaście, czternaście, piętnaście, szesnaście, siedemnaście, osiemnaście, dziewiętnaście. Note the spellings piętnaście and dziewiętnaście (ę, not ięć), and that -naście is stressed on the a: dwa-NAŚ-cie.

rules.title: Tens, hundreds and thousands
rules.body: dwadzieścia (20), trzydzieści (30), czterdzieści (40), pięćdziesiąt (50), sześćdziesiąt, siedemdziesiąt, osiemdziesiąt, dziewięćdziesiąt; sto (100), dwieście (200), trzysta, czterysta, pięćset, sześćset, siedemset, osiemset, dziewięćset; tysiąc (1000), dwa tysiące, pięć tysięcy; milion. Compound numbers are simply strung together: dwadzieścia jeden (21), sto pięćdziesiąt trzy (153), tysiąc dziewięćset (1900).

rules.title: One and two agree in gender
rules.body: jeden behaves like an adjective: jeden dom, jedna kawa, jedno piwo. Two is dwa with masculine and neuter nouns (dwa koty, dwa okna) and dwie with feminine nouns (dwie kobiety, dwie kawy). Counting male persons has its own forms: dwaj studenci or dwóch studentów, trzej / trzech, czterej / czterech, and from five the genitive form of the number: pięciu studentów, dziesięciu mężczyzn.

examples.target: jeden dom, jedna kawa, jedno piwo
examples.en: one house, one coffee, one beer

rules.title: Counting rule and verb agreement
rules.body: After 2, 3, 4 (and compounds ending in them, like 22, 33, 104) the noun is nominative plural and the verb is plural: Dwa koty śpią. Trzy kobiety pracują. After 5 and up, including all of 11-19 and compounds ending in 0, 1 and 5-9, the noun is genitive plural and the verb is third person singular, in the past tense neuter: Pięć kotów śpi. Dziesięć kobiet pracowało. Dwanaście osób czeka. The same applies after ile, kilka (a few), wiele, dużo.

rules.title: Ordinal numbers
rules.body: pierwszy (1st), drugi, trzeci, czwarty, piąty, szósty, siódmy, ósmy, dziewiąty, dziesiąty, jedenasty, dwunasty, trzynasty, czternasty, piętnasty, szesnasty, siedemnasty, osiemnasty, dziewiętnasty, dwudziesty (20th), trzydziesty, czterdziesty, pięćdziesiąty, setny (100th). They decline like adjectives: pierwsza lekcja, drugie piwo, na trzecim piętrze. In 21-99 both parts are ordinal: dwudziesty pierwszy (21st), trzydziesta druga (32nd). In writing a dot marks an ordinal: 3. = trzeci.

examples.en: I live on the third floor.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Która (jest) godzina? (What time is it?). Hours are feminine ordinals agreeing with godzina: Jest pierwsza. Jest druga. Jest dziesiąta. Half past uses wpół do + the genitive of the NEXT hour: wpół do trzeciej = 2:30. Minutes past: piętnaście po drugiej (2:15), dziesięć po ósmej. Minutes to: za piętnaście trzecia (2:45), za pięć dziewiąta. Timetables and official speech use the 24-hour clock with a cardinal for the minutes: trzynasta czterdzieści (13:40), dwudziesta (20:00). Everyday: druga trzydzieści.

examples.en: It is a quarter to eight.

rules.title: At what time?
rules.body: At a time is o + locative of the feminine ordinal: o pierwszej, o drugiej, o wpół do trzeciej, o dziesiątej. O której (godzinie)? = At what time? From ... to ... is od ... do ... with the genitive: od ósmej do czwartej. Parts of the day are added as adverbs: rano (in the morning), po południu (in the afternoon), wieczorem (in the evening), w nocy (at night): o siódmej rano, o ósmej wieczorem.

examples.target: O której jest lekcja? O dziewiątej.
examples.en: What time is the lesson? At nine.

examples.target: Spotkamy się o wpół do siódmej.
examples.en: We'll meet at half past six.
I work from eight to four.

rules.title: Days of the week and on
rules.body: poniedziałek, wtorek, środa, czwartek, piątek, sobota, niedziela; day names are written in lower case. On a day is w / we + accusative: w poniedziałek, we wtorek, w środę, w czwartek, w piątek, w sobotę, w niedzielę. Every is co: co poniedziałek, co tydzień; at the weekend is w weekend. Jaki dzisiaj jest dzień? Dzisiaj jest środa.

examples.en: On Saturday I'm going to the cinema.
On Tuesday I have a lesson.

examples.target: Co niedzielę jemy obiad u babci.
examples.en: Every Sunday we have dinner at grandma's.

rules.title: Months and in
rules.body: styczeń, luty, marzec, kwiecień, maj, czerwiec, lipiec, sierpień, wrzesień, październik, listopad, grudzień; written in lower case. In a month is w + locative: w styczniu, w lutym, w marcu, w kwietniu, w maju, w czerwcu, w lipcu, w sierpniu, we wrześniu, w październiku, w listopadzie, w grudniu. The genitive, needed for dates: stycznia, lutego, marca, kwietnia, maja, czerwca, lipca, sierpnia, września, października, listopada, grudnia. Seasons use the instrumental: wiosną, latem, jesienią, zimą.

examples.en: In summer I go to the seaside.

rules.title: Dates, years, age and money
rules.body: Który jest dzisiaj? (What's the date?) Dzisiaj jest piąty maja: a masculine ordinal (dzień is understood) plus the month in the genitive. On a date puts the ordinal in the genitive too: piątego maja, dwudziestego pierwszego marca; Urodziłam się trzeciego lipca. Years: in 2020 = w dwa tysiące dwudziestym roku; only the last part is an ordinal in the locative: w tysiąc dziewięćset osiemdziesiątym dziewiątym roku (in 1989). Age: Mam dwadzieścia lat, with rok (1), lata (2-4), lat (5 and up). Money: jeden złoty, dwa złote, pięć złotych; jeden grosz, dwa grosze, pięć groszy.

examples.en: Today is the first of September.
I (m) was born on the tenth of February.

exercises.q: five =
exercises.explain: pięć is the cardinal five; piąty is fifth.

exercises.q: Write the number 7 in Polish: ___
exercises.explain: siedem is seven; siódmy is seventh.

exercises.q: jeden agrees with the noun: jeden dom, jedna kawa, jedno piwo.
exercises.explain: jeden behaves like an adjective and takes gender endings.

exercises.q: two women =
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns take dwie, and after 2 the noun is nominative plural.

exercises.q: Mam ___ lat. (twenty)
exercises.explain: dwadzieścia is twenty, and lat is the genitive plural of rok.

exercises.q: It is three o'clock =
exercises.explain: Hours are feminine ordinals agreeing with godzina: trzecia.

exercises.q: Jest ___ do trzeciej. (It is half past two)
exercises.explain: Half past is wpół do plus the genitive of the next hour.

exercises.q: wpół do trzeciej means 2:30.
exercises.explain: wpół do names the hour that is coming: halfway to three.

exercises.q: Which form of kot follows pięć?
exercises.explain: From five up the noun is in the genitive plural.

exercises.q: Spotkamy się o ___. (at five o'clock: piąta in the locative)
exercises.explain: o takes the locative; feminine ordinals end in -ej there.

exercises.en: We're meeting at seven in the evening.

exercises.q: dwanaście kotów is correct because the numbers 11-19 take the genitive plural.
exercises.explain: All the -naście numbers behave like five and up, even dwanaście and czternaście.

exercises.q: on Monday =
exercises.explain: Days take w plus the accusative, which for poniedziałek equals the nominative.

exercises.q: Idę do kina w ___. (on Saturday: sobota)
exercises.explain: w plus the accusative: the feminine -a becomes -ę.

exercises.q: in March =
exercises.explain: w takes the locative; marzec loses its fleeting e and takes -u: w marcu.

exercises.q: Dzisiaj jest piąty ___. (May: maj in the genitive)
exercises.explain: In dates the month is in the genitive: piąty maja.

exercises.q: In the date piąty maja the month is in the genitive.
exercises.explain: The date is literally the fifth (day) of May, so the month takes the genitive.

exercises.en: I (a woman) was born on the third of July.

exercises.q: on the 21st of March =
exercises.explain: Both parts of the ordinal go into the genitive, and the month is genitive too.

exercises.q: Mam trzy ___. (years: the form of rok after 3)
exercises.explain: rok has the plural lata after 2-4 and lat after 5 and up.

exercises.q: Pięć kotów śpią is correct.
exercises.explain: After five and up the verb is singular: Pięć kotów śpi.

exercises.q: a quarter to three =
exercises.explain: Minutes to the hour use za plus the minutes plus the coming hour in the nominative.

exercises.q: To kosztuje pięć ___. (złoty, genitive plural)
exercises.explain: złoty declines like an adjective: dwa złote, pięć złotych.

exercises.en: I work from eight to four.

exercises.q: Ten women were working =
exercises.explain: After ten the noun is genitive plural and the past-tense verb is neuter singular.

exercises.q: W ___ jest zimno. (in February: luty in the locative)
exercises.explain: luty declines like an adjective: w lutym.

exercises.q: Month names are capitalised in Polish, as they are in English.
exercises.explain: Months and days are written in lower case: maj, grudzień, sobota.

exercises.q: five students (male) =
exercises.explain: Male persons use the special form of the number plus the genitive plural: pięciu studentów.
